strengths: The core idea—casting dense-to-MoE conversion as a differentiable dynamic structural pruning problem, learned only through lightweight router/projection/hypernetwork modules while freezing the original weights—is an interesting and reasonably novel angle on both compression and MoE construction that avoids expensive continued pretraining (e.g., contrasts favorably with LLaMA-MoE's 200B-token training).

Extensive empirical evaluation across many model families (LLaMA-2 7B/13B, LLaMA-3 8B, Qwen-2.5 7B/14B, Phi-2) and multiple active-parameter budgets (40-80%), consistently outperforming a wide range of strong structural- and semi-structural-pruning baselines (DISP-LLM, ModeGPT, LLM Surgeon, SliceGPT, SparseGPT, Wanda, Pruner-Zero) in both perplexity and zero-shot accuracy, without any fine-tuning of backbone weights.
The regularization design (union-of-experts, parameter/width regularization, load-balancing) is well-motivated and each component's effect is examined via training dynamics plots and ablations.

Good engineering details for reproducibility: explicit hyperparameters, module structures, a table of additional parameter counts (shown to be <0.3% overhead), and an efficient O(T/N)-reduction trick for the union regularization.
Thoughtful analysis extras: layer-wise width visualization, expert similarity heatmaps, training-cost comparison in USD, and qualitative expert-routing visualizations that add some interpretability.
weaknesses: No actual latency/throughput measurements are reported; the entire efficiency argument rests on 'active parameter count' as a proxy, but token-dependent MLP expert routing and per-token top-k head selection could introduce nontrivial overhead (irregular memory access, batching complications) that the paper does not measure or discuss on real hardware, undermining the central efficiency claim.

The framing of the method as producing an MoE with 'meaningful experts...inherently existing within dense models' is somewhat overstated: the experts are non-overlapping structural subsets carved from shared original weight matrices via masking, which is conceptually closer to token-conditional structured pruning than to true independently specialized MoE experts; the qualitative visualizations (Tables 8-9, App. E) show largely identical routing patterns across many experts for generic text, weakening the 'meaningful expert' narrative except in a cherry-picked math example.

No direct experimental comparison to actual dense-to-MoE conversion baselines like LLaMA-MoE, despite being discussed at length in related work; the comparisons are exclusively against static/dynamic structural pruning methods, which is a somewhat different problem class and may make the 'MoE' contribution harder to assess on its own terms.

Hyperparameter sensitivity (α, β, γ, temperature τ, bias b) is fixed across all experiments/models without ablation showing robustness, and the interaction between these several regularizers is complex and only partially explained.

Some baseline comparisons mix fine-tuned (Alpaca-tuned) and non-fine-tuned variants inconsistently across tables/models, which slightly complicates fair apples-to-apples comparison even though ToMoE itself needs no fine-tuning.

The self-distillation training still requires holding the full dense model in memory/compute during training (teacher forward pass), so while GPU memory overhead is claimed to be avoided via in-place computation, the overall computational/training cost relative to simpler post-training pruning methods (e.g., magnitude/Wanda-style one-shot pruning) is understated in the main comparisons (Fig. 5b only benchmarks against other learning-based methods).

strengths: The paper tackles a practically relevant problem (bridging the performance gap left by structural pruning) and proposes a reasonably elegant unification of dynamic pruning and MoE construction using differentiable Gumbel-based selection, hypernetwork-generated expert embeddings, and several well-motivated regularizers (union-of-experts, parameter budget, load balancing).

Broad empirical coverage across multiple model families and scales (Phi-2, LLaMA-2 7B/13B, LLaMA-3 8B, Qwen-2.5 7B/14B) and multiple sparsity levels (40-75% active parameters), with comparisons to a large number of recent structural- and semi-structural-pruning baselines.

Reported perplexity and zero-shot accuracy numbers are consistently favorable relative to strong recent baselines (DISP-LLM, ModeGPT, LLM Surgeon), and the method requires no fine-tuning of the base weights and reports lower or comparable training cost than other learning-based pruning approaches.

Reasonably detailed appendix with ablations (loss components, dataset choice), training dynamics, expert visualization, and analytical discussion of parameter/architecture design (e.g., handling of RoPE sub-spaces for head pruning), which aids some reproducibility.

The idea that meaningful expert-like substructures can be uncovered inside dense MLPs without weight updates is an interesting empirical observation, complementary to expert-construction methods that require costly continued pretraining (e.g., LLaMA-MoE).
weaknesses: The central motivation of the paper is efficient serving/deployment, yet no actual wall-clock latency, throughput, or memory measurements of the resulting MoE model are reported anywhere -- only "active parameter percentage" and a training-cost-in-dollars comparison (Fig. 5b). Because MLP experts use top-1 per-token routing and MHA uses per-token selection matrices S_t, actual inference requires gather/scatter operations across tokens with potentially different active weight subsets; whether this translates into real speedups over the claimed 'fixed budget' is never empirically verified, which undermines the core deployment claim.

The MHA "dynamic top-K routing" is somewhat misleadingly framed: the paper states that after training, K is fixed via rounding an average computed on a data subset and used for top-K routing at inference, meaning attention head/dimension budgets are effectively static per layer, not truly adaptive per input the way MoE routing is; the distinction between this and standard structural pruning is not clearly substantiated by the framing as "MHA with Top-k routing."

Directly relevant prior work on discovering/extracting expert-like substructures from dense FFNs without continued pretraining (e.g., MoEfication-style approaches that cluster/split FFN neurons into experts) is not discussed or compared, which weakens the novelty claim that "these results represent a novel contribution that has not been demonstrated in previous studies." LLaMA-MoE is discussed qualitatively but never empirically compared despite being the most conceptually similar dense-to-MoE baseline mentioned in Related Work.

No variance/multiple-seed reporting despite training relying on stochastic Gumbel-Softmax/Sigmoid sampling; given the many interacting regularization terms and hyperparameters (α, β, γ, b, τ, p), the sensitivity and stability of the method to these choices is not analyzed beyond a small ablation on one model, raising reproducibility concerns.

Some baseline comparisons appear potentially confounded by differing calibration/training data (e.g., "+Alpaca" variants vs. base variants of competing methods, and ToMoE's own use of a WikiText+Alpaca+Code-Alpaca mixture), making it difficult to attribute performance gains cleanly to the proposed dynamic-pruning-to-MoE mechanism rather than to data mixture choices.

Evaluation is restricted to five common-sense/reasoning zero-shot benchmarks and WikiText-2 perplexity; there is no evaluation on generation quality, longer-form reasoning, or instruction-following tasks, despite training data including Alpaca/Code-Alpaca, which limits confidence that the approach generalizes broadly.

The expert visualization results (Tables 8-9, Fig. 9) are qualitative and based on a very small number of hand-picked examples; claims about syntax vs. semantic specialization of experts are speculative and not rigorously quantified.

strengths: Novel and reasonably well-motivated idea: reformulating structural pruning as a route to a fixed-budget MoE model rather than permanently deleting weights, unifying dynamic pruning and MoE construction under one differentiable framework.

Broad and consistent empirical validation across many model families and scales (Phi-2, LLaMA-2 7B/13B, LLaMA-3 8B, Qwen-2.5 7B/14B) and against a large set of strong, recent baselines (DISP-LLM, ModeGPT, LLM Surgeon, SliceGPT, semi-structured methods), with ToMoE consistently achieving lower perplexity and higher zero-shot accuracy at matched or fewer active parameters.

The method is training-cheap (comparable to or cheaper than other learning-based pruning baselines, per Fig. 5b) and does not require the original weights to be updated, enabling in-place self-knowledge distillation without extra memory overhead.

Reasonably thorough ablations and analyses (training dynamics under different active-parameter ratios, loss-component ablations, expert-width visualizations, expert-similarity heatmaps, and qualitative token-routing visualizations) that lend some insight into why the method works.

Careful engineering details for making the approach practical: RoPE-compatible head-dimension pruning, an efficient reformulation of the union-of-experts regularizer, and a pseudo-MoE equivalence that simplifies training/inference.
weaknesses: No actual wall-clock inference latency/throughput measurements are provided; despite motivating the method by 'consistent computational costs' and ease of serving relative to token-dependent dynamic pruning, the paper never empirically demonstrates real inference speedups or serving benefits over the structural-pruning baselines it compares against.

Evaluation is restricted to perplexity and five standard zero-shot commonsense/QA benchmarks; despite training with a code-mixed dataset, no code-generation, math, or generative quality evaluations are reported, limiting evidence of general capability retention.

No mention of code/checkpoint release, and the pipeline involves several interacting non-trivial components (hypernetwork, multiple projection heads, Gumbel-Softmax/Sigmoid temperatures, several regularization coefficients tuned per active-parameter ratio) — reproducibility by others without released code is likely to be difficult.

Key hyperparameters (α, β, γ) are reported as fixed across all models/settings with essentially no sensitivity analysis, and results appear to be single-run (no variance reported) despite the stochastic Gumbel-based training, making it hard to judge robustness.

Comparisons are somewhat inconsistent in fine-tuning/data-augmentation conditions: some baselines are shown with '-Alpaca' fine-tuning while ToMoE's own mixed-dataset training procedure is not always clearly matched against the same condition in each table, making some head-to-head comparisons less clean.

The strong claim that 'MoEs inherently exist within dense models' is largely supported by qualitative visualizations (a few example sentences) rather than a rigorous, quantitative characterization of expert specialization; the token-routing patterns shown appear largely syntactic/positional rather than clearly semantic, which somewhat undercuts the framing.

The number of experts N is only varied in one setting (Qwen-2.5 7B); it is unclear how sensitive the method is to N and how this interacts with different model architectures or the top-1 routing choice for MLP versus top-k for attention heads.

strengths: Novel and technically interesting reframing of dense-to-MoE conversion as a differentiable dynamic structural pruning problem, unifying expert construction and router training in a single stage without any weight updates, which is a meaningful departure from prior two-stage MoEfication/continual-pretraining approaches.

Extensive experimental validation across many base models (Phi-2, LLaMA-2 7B/13B, LLaMA-3 8B, Qwen-2.5 7B/14B) and a wide range of compression ratios, compared against a large and relevant set of baselines spanning structural pruning, semi-structural pruning, and MoE-construction methods.

Consistent and often substantial performance improvements over strong recent baselines (DISP-LLM, ModeGPT, LLM Surgeon, LLaMA-MoE, LLaMA-MoE-v2, CMoE) while requiring drastically fewer training tokens/iterations and no fine-tuning of backbone weights, which is a practically appealing efficiency property.
Thorough set of regularizations (union-of-experts, parameter budget, load balancing) with clear motivations and reasonably careful ablations isolating their individual contributions.

Good engineering/analysis depth: training dynamics, cost comparisons in dollar terms, non-uniform width allocation across layers, expert similarity visualization, and design justification for why dynamic pruning is applied only to V/O and not Q/K (Appendix F) demonstrate care in the design process.
In-place self-knowledge distillation avoids extra memory overhead, and the additional trainable parameter count is shown to be small (~0.27% of model size for LLaMA-2 7B).
weaknesses: The qualitative expert-visualization evidence (Tables 7, 11, 14) is weak: the highlighted colored spans across 'different experts' correspond to nearly identical continuations for the same prompt, and the claim that experts capture syntactic/semantic specialization is asserted rather than quantitatively substantiated (e.g., no statistical or probing analysis to support the comparison to Jiang et al. 2024).

The method introduces a fairly large number of hyperparameters (α, β, γ, τ, bias b, embedding dimension, GRU hypernetwork size) but sensitivity analysis is limited mostly to τ over a narrow range; there is little discussion of how sensitive results are to α/β/γ across models or ratios.

Some cross-method comparisons (e.g., Tables 5–6 against LLaMA-MoE/LLaMA-MoE-v2/CMoE) contrast token budgets that differ by orders of magnitude (0.02B vs. multiple billions of tokens), which is presented as an unambiguous advantage, but the fairness of comparing a frozen-weight router-only method against continually pretrained MoE baselines trained with very different optimization objectives could be discussed more critically rather than framed as straightforward superiority.

Because the parameter regularization pushes toward a specific target ratio p, the model must be retrained separately for each active-parameter budget, unlike some baselines that offer more flexible/elastic deployment; this limitation is not explicitly discussed.

Inference throughput gains (Table 15) are relatively modest and at smaller batch sizes are actually lower than the LLaMA-MoE baseline, somewhat undercutting the efficiency narrative built around per-token top-K attention routing; this discrepancy is not analyzed in depth.

The theoretical claim that 'MoE inherently exists within dense models' is largely an empirical assertion motivated by good downstream numbers rather than a rigorously argued or theoretically grounded mechanism, and the paper would benefit from stronger conceptual grounding or ablation isolating this claim from optimization/regularization effects.

Reproducibility depends heavily on many implementation details (Appendix A–C) and a promised but not fully specified code release, and the pipeline's complexity (hypernetwork, multiple projection modules, Gumbel-based discrete relaxations with specific temperature/bias settings) may make faithful reproduction by others nontrivial.

strengths: The paper tackles a well-motivated problem (bridging the performance gap between structural pruning and MoE construction) and proposes a technically interesting unification of dynamic structural pruning with router learning, avoiding the two-stage expert-construction/router-training pipeline used by prior MoE-conversion works.

Very broad empirical coverage: results are reported across many backbones (Phi-2, LLaMA-2 7B/13B, LLaMA-3 8B, Qwen-2.5 7B/14B) and a large number of competing structural pruning, semi-structural pruning, and MoE-construction baselines, at multiple sparsity levels.

The method requires no weight updates to the backbone (only lightweight router/projection/hypernetwork parameters are trained), which is presented as a practical advantage in terms of training cost, and the paper supports this with an explicit dollar-cost comparison (Fig. 6b).

The paper includes a reasonably thorough analysis section (training dynamics, ablations on loss terms and dataset choice, expert-width visualization, expert-similarity heatmaps, token-routing visualizations, throughput measurements), which is helpful for understanding some of the mechanics of the method.

The theoretical discussion in Appendix F, motivating why dynamic pruning is applied to V/O but static pruning to Q/K due to RoPE and attention-score consistency issues, is a nice piece of reasoning that adds some rigor to a design choice that could otherwise seem arbitrary.
weaknesses: The abstract/introduction claims the method 'consistently outperforms' prior MoE-construction and pruning techniques, but this is contradicted by the paper's own Table 6, where ToMoE (57.40 average) underperforms both LLaMA-MoE-v2 variants (59.61 and 59.31 average) on LLaMA-3 8B despite using far fewer tokens; this inconsistency is not acknowledged or discussed in the text, which otherwise frames all comparisons as favorable to ToMoE.

The qualitative visualizations in Tables 7, 11, and 14 show essentially identical highlighted token-to-expert assignments across three different MLP layers (layer 1, 16, 32) for the same input text, which is implausible if experts/routing genuinely differ across layers; this raises concerns about the correctness or care taken in producing these figures, and undermines confidence in the qualitative claims made about expert specialization.

The central narrative claim that 'MoE inherently exists within dense models' is a strong interpretive claim, yet the paper's own analysis (Sec 4.4, Table 7) finds that experts align with syntax rather than semantics, which is a considerably weaker and more mundane finding than what the framing implies; the gap between the claimed contribution and the actual evidence is not adequately reconciled.

Several baseline comparisons are pulled directly from other papers' reported numbers rather than reproduced under a controlled, identical setup (same calibration data, same evaluation harness version, same prompt formatting); given how sensitive pruning results can be to such details, it is unclear how much of the improvement is attributable to the method itself versus differences in comparison protocol.

Hyperparameters (α=16, β=2.0, γ=1.0, τ=0.4, temperature/bias constants in Gumbel relaxations) are fixed identically across models ranging from ~2.7B to ~14B parameters and across very different architectures (Phi-2, LLaMA, Qwen), with no sensitivity study showing that this fixed configuration is actually near-optimal for each model; this raises reproducibility and generality concerns, especially since the training objective already has four competing loss terms whose interactions (e.g., RP and RL 'creating an interesting phenomenon') are only qualitatively described.

The paper repeatedly asserts the method needs 'no fine-tuning' and 'no weight updates,' but training still requires a KL-based self-distillation procedure on a specific corpus (WikiText/Alpaca/Code-Alpaca) for 10,000 iterations on 1-4 A100 GPUs to learn routers/hypernetwork/projections; this is a real training cost that is somewhat downplayed relative to competing 'training-free' pruning baselines (e.g., SliceGPT, Wanda) that require no gradient-based optimization at all.

The code repository link in the abstract is left blank ('The code for this paper is available at'), and several implementation details (e.g., exact choice of K for top-K attention routing at inference, sensitivity of results to the fixed random hypernetwork input z) are only partially specified, which could hinder independent reproduction.

No variance/standard deviation over multiple seeds is reported for any of the zero-shot task numbers, despite the use of stochastic Gumbel-based relaxations during training, making it hard to assess whether the reported improvements over close competitors (e.g., DISP-LLM, ModeGPT) are robust or within noise.

strengths: The paper introduces a novel single-stage formulation that unifies expert construction and router training via differentiable dynamic structural pruning, in contrast to prior MoE-from-dense approaches (e.g., LLaMA-MoE, MoEfication) that separate these stages and typically require continued pretraining/fine-tuning.

Extensive empirical evaluation spanning four model families (Phi-2, LLaMA-2 7B/13B, LLaMA-3 8B, Qwen-2.5 7B/14B) and comparisons against a wide range of baselines: structural pruning (LLM-Pruner, ShortGPT, SLEB, SliceGPT, ModeGPT, LLM Surgeon, DISP-LLM), semi-structured pruning (SparseGPT, Wanda, Pruner-Zero), and MoE-conversion methods (LLaMA-MoE, LLaMA-MoE-v2, CMoE, G-MoEfication).

Method is training-efficient: original weights are frozen, only a small router/hypernetwork/projection module is trained (~0.27% additional parameters for LLaMA-2 7B), and self-knowledge distillation is performed in-place without loading a second model, giving favorable cost/token-budget comparisons (Tab. 5/6, Fig. 6b).

Thorough ablation and analysis: training dynamics under different active-parameter ratios, ablations on loss components (RU, self-KD, dataset mixture), sensitivity to temperature τ, justification of design choices for MHA pruning (Appendix F), throughput benchmarking, and visualizations of expert width/similarity/token routing.

The regularization design (union-of-experts, parameter, load-balancing) is well-motivated and its interactions are empirically examined (e.g., Fig. 6a showing near-full parameter coverage despite non-uniform widths).
weaknesses: The central narrative claim that 'MoE inherently exists within dense models' and experts encode meaningful specialization is only weakly supported: the token-routing visualizations (Tab. 7, 11) show no clear semantic pattern for general text, and the authors themselves state that experts 'align syntax rather than semantic meanings' and that 'further investigation is required'—this undercuts a key motivating claim of the paper.

Not all results support the 'consistently outperforms' framing: in Table 6, ToMoE underperforms fully-trained LLaMA-MoE-v2 on average (57.40 vs 59.61/59.31) despite the text characterizing this as 'comparable performance,' which is a favorable framing that should be tempered.

Reported experimental comparisons mix substantially different training budgets (e.g., Tab. 5/6 compare a method trained with ~0.02B tokens against baselines trained with 1.2B–7B tokens), which, while favorable to demonstrating efficiency, makes it harder to disentangle whether gains stem from the proposed architecture/loss design versus simply avoiding expensive fine-tuning; a controlled comparison at matched compute would strengthen the claims.

No statistical significance testing or repeated-seed variance is reported despite using stochastic Gumbel-based sampling (ST-GSig/ST-GSmax) during training, leaving open questions about training stability and result variance.

Hyperparameters (α=16, β=2, γ=1, τ=0.4, b=3.0) are fixed globally across all models/settings with only limited sensitivity analysis (only τ is ablated), raising reproducibility and generalization concerns for new model families or compression ratios.

The abstract states 'the code for this paper is available at' with no actual link provided in the manuscript, which is a reproducibility concern; combined with the complexity of the method (hypernetwork, multiple per-layer projection modules, several regularizers), independent reproduction may be nontrivial without released code.

Evaluation is limited to perplexity and multiple-choice zero/few-shot benchmarks; no evaluation on open-ended generation, instruction-following, or downstream task quality is provided, which is relevant since the paper targets practical LLM deployment.
